---
title: "Audit Monitoring and Report Assurance"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Distinguish continuous auditing from continuous monitoring, and exceptions from anomalies, and specify a monitoring test by its rule, population, frequency, and expected result.
2. Build an exception register in Power Query that turns the flags of several tests into one table of exceptions, with a table of tests and the populations needed for rates.
3. Build a monitoring page that shows exception counts and rates by test and month and lets a reviewer drill through to the documents behind them.
4. Record a disposition for each exception in a table that survives every refresh, and decide which open exceptions a reviewer should examine first.
5. Test a report before relying on it, by reconciling its populations, rerunning its tests, and establishing the date through which its data run.
6. Explain the change controls that a report used every month needs, and why copies of its file escape them.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

It is May 2027, and you are back on the internal audit team of Chapters 8 and 12. The chief audit executive brings three requests. The first comes from the audit committee. The tests of Chapters 8 and 12 found journal entries approved by the people who created them, purchase orders approved after the approver had left the company, and pay approved by the employee being paid. The committee wants to know every month whether such exceptions recur, rather than wait for the next annual review. The second is the chief audit executive's own. A monthly report is useful only if each exception is reviewed once and the conclusion kept, so that next month's review starts from the exceptions still open rather than from the beginning. The third comes from the controller, who now presents Charles River Reports, the package of Chapters 13 to 15, at the managers' monthly meeting, plans to give each manager access of their own, and asks whether internal audit can rely on it too.

Your task is to build a monitoring report for internal audit, to record and prioritize the review of its exceptions, and to test both reports before anyone relies on them. This chapter teaches continuous monitoring and the design of an exception register, a monitoring page that leads from exception counts to documents, the review of exceptions over time, and the audit of a report itself: its populations, its tests, the currency of its data, and the control of changes to it. How a report is published, secured, and shared, which needs a Power BI license to practice in full, is the subject of [the appendix on publishing and security](#sec-appendix-publishing).


## From Audit Tests to Monitoring

Chapter 8 tested whole populations once, in a workbook, and Chapter 12 saved its tests as a library of queries that the team could run again every quarter. Monitoring takes the next step: the same tests run every period, on new data, with the results kept and compared over time. Vasarhelyi and Halper (1991) described one of the first such systems, built for the internal auditors of AT&T Bell Laboratories, which measured key figures of large systems, compared them with standards, and called the auditors' attention to problems as they arose. Two decades later, continuous auditing had moved from research into practice in many firms (Alles et al., 2008).

Two terms describe this work, and they differ in who does it. Continuous auditing is internal audit's use of technology to assess risks and controls on an ongoing basis, so that it can give the board and management assurance throughout the year rather than once (Institute of Internal Auditors [IIA], 2025). Continuous monitoring is management's own ongoing review of whether its controls operate as designed. Many auditors hold that monitoring belongs to management, not to internal audit, but effective continuous auditing depends on strong monitoring, and internal audit can help a business build it (Tronto & Killingsworth, 2021). In this chapter you build a monitoring report as internal audit's tool, and the same tests could be handed to management to run as its own monitoring.

Monitoring tests are of two kinds. Kogan et al. (2014) separate a first layer that checks deterministic business rules, such as an approval within the approver's limit, from a second layer of analytical monitoring that looks for unusual patterns. A rule either holds or fails, and a failure is an exception in the sense of Chapter 8, a record that meets a test's criteria and therefore needs an explanation. An analytical test produces anomalies: records or periods that differ from what is expected, such as two payments of the same amount to the same supplier a few days apart, or first digits that depart from Benford's Law. An anomaly is a reason to look, not yet a failure. The exception register you build in this chapter holds the rule tests; the anomaly tests of Chapters 8 and 12 return in the exercises.

A monitoring system that runs every month can produce more exceptions than anyone can review, a problem this chapter returns to once the register is built. A practical first defense is design. Each test should state its rule, its population, and the result expected, as the comment above each query of Chapter 12's audit query library did, and also how often it runs, so that a reviewer can tell an expected exception from a new one. Metcash, an Australian distributor, ran more than a hundred automated tests daily, with an integrated system for managing their exceptions and visual reports for reviewing them (Hardy & Laslett, 2015). @tbl-16-01 lists the tests of this chapter, all of them rules that the book has already run once, each with the process whose documents it tests and where it was first run.

| TestID | Test | Process | Source |
|------------|------------------------------|--------------|------|
| JE Weekend | Entry created on a weekend | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE Backdated | Entry created after its posting date | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE SelfApproved | Entry approved by its creator | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE AboveLimit | Entry above its approver's limit | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| JE RoundAmount | Entry in whole thousands | Journal entries | Chapter 8 |
| PO SelfApproved | Order approved by its creator | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PO AboveLimit | Order above its approver's limit | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PO AfterTermination | Order approved after the approver left | Purchase orders | Chapter 12 |
| PR PaidBeforeApproval | Pay made before the register was approved | Payroll | Exercise 12.5 |
| PR AfterTermination | Pay period ending after termination | Payroll | Exercise 12.5 |
| PR SelfApproved | Register approved by its own employee | Payroll | Exercise 12.5 |

: The monitoring tests {#tbl-16-01}

Who sees the results matters too. Gonzalez and Hoffman (2018) found in an experiment that telling people promptly which of their transactions a monitoring system had flagged also told them what it could not detect, and that when the system was weak, prompt notification made participants more inclined to commit fraud. A monitoring report therefore belongs with internal audit's audit workpapers. It goes to the people who oversee the controls, not to the people whose approvals it tests, which is why this chapter builds it in a file of its own rather than as pages of the controller's package. @fig-16-01 shows the cycle a monitoring test follows.

![The Monitoring Cycle.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-01-monitoring-cycle.svg){#fig-16-01 fig-alt="A cycle diagram. A rule runs on each period's population and produces exceptions; the exceptions go to internal audit's monitoring report, where each receives a disposition; dispositions feed back into the rule, its threshold, or the control. A side panel distinguishes continuous auditing, run by internal audit for assurance, from continuous monitoring, run by management on its own controls, and notes that the exceptions go to the people who oversee the controls, not to those whose transactions are tested."}


## Designing an Exception Register

An exception register is a single table that holds the exceptions of every monitoring test, one row for each exception of each test, with the same columns whatever the test: the test that found it, the document, its date, its amount, and the employee responsible, here the approver. Chapter 12 built the same thing in SQL, when UNION ALL stacked the exceptions of several queries into one result, each labeled with the test that found it. In Power BI the register is built in Power Query, so that every refresh runs the tests again on the new data. @tbl-16-02 shows where each column comes from in the three processes this chapter monitors.

| Register column | Journal entries | Purchase orders | Payroll registers |
|------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| TestID | JE and the flag name | PO and the flag name | PR and the flag name |
| DocumentNumber | EntryNumber | PONumber | Register and its ID |
| EventDate | PostingDate | OrderDate | PayDate |
| Amount | TotalAmount | OrderTotal | NetPay |
| EmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID | ApprovedByEmployeeID |

: The columns of the exception register {#tbl-16-02}

The register takes three moves. First, each test becomes a flag column, 1 if the record fails the rule and 0 if it passes, the Power Query counterpart of the flag formulas Chapter 8 wrote in the columns of an Excel table, and the flags of a document add up to its risk score. Second, unpivoting turns the flag columns of a table into rows. Each record becomes one row per flag, with the flag's name in a column named Attribute and its value in a column named Value (Microsoft, 2025), and keeping only the rows whose value is 1 leaves exactly the exceptions. Third, appending stacks the exception tables of the three processes into one (Microsoft, 2026a). Append is Power Query's counterpart of UNION ALL, with one difference that matters: UNION ALL matches columns by their position, while Append matches them by their names, and a column that one table lacks is filled with nulls. Each exception table must therefore rename its columns to the register's names before the append, or the result has a DocumentNumber column that is empty for one process and a PONumber column that is empty for the others.

A count of exceptions means little without the size of the population it came from. A dozen exceptions among a few hundred journal entries and a dozen among many thousands of purchase orders are very different rates. The register therefore sits beside the populations it tests, which stay in the model as fact tables of their own, and a measure divides the exceptions of each test by the documents of its process. The populations are also what the auditor reconciles before relying on the tests, as Chapters 8 and 12 did: if the journal entries in the model do not add up to the journal entry postings in the ledger, the monitoring is testing an incomplete population. @fig-16-02 shows the model.

![The Exception Register in the Monitoring Model.](/visuals/svg/fig-16-02-exception-register.svg){#fig-16-02 fig-alt="A model diagram. Three flagged tables, JournalEntry, PurchaseOrder, and PayrollRegister, each feed an exception query through Unpivot and a filter on the flag value; the three exception queries are appended into one Exceptions table. Exceptions relates to Tests on TestID, to Date on EventDate, and to Employee on EmployeeID. The three flagged tables remain in the model as populations, related to Date, and JournalLines relates to JournalEntry."}


{{< include _tutorial-01.qmd >}}


## The Monitoring Page

A monitoring page answers three questions in order: which tests are failing, when, and on which documents. A matrix with the tests as rows and the months as columns, each cell holding the number of exceptions, answers the first two at a glance. Shading the cells by rule, darker for more exceptions, turns the matrix into a heat map, in which a row of dark cells and a column of dark cells mean different things. The number stays in each cell, so the shading never carries the meaning alone, the rule Chapters 4 and 6 set for conditional formats and charts and Chapter 13 applied to every visual. How well a reviewer reads such a display depends on the visual chosen as well as on the reviewer: in a study by Baaske et al. (2025), participants who chose better visualizations identified anomalies more accurately.

Charles River's register shows both patterns. Most of the journal entry and purchase order exceptions fall in January, in each of the three years, and so do five of the six payroll exceptions outside one recurring test. A cluster in the same month of every year points to how the controls operate at that time of year, when the first entries, orders, and payrolls of a new year are processed, and it tells the auditor where to look and when. One test behaves differently: registers approved by the employee they pay appear in every month, because one employee approves every register, including the approver's own. An exception that recurs in every period is not a lapse to be explained one document at a time. It points to the design of the control, which gives no one the task of approving the approver's pay. The concentration of approval that Chapter 12 found for purchase orders, and Exercise 12.5 for payroll, reappears when the exceptions are counted by approver.

The rate puts each count beside its population. Journal entries are few, so even a handful of exceptions is a high rate, while purchase orders run to many thousands and their exceptions are a small fraction. Rates per thousand documents let a reviewer see whether a process is getting better or worse as its volume changes, which a count alone hides. Over the three years, the rate for journal entries fell and rose again, the rate for purchase orders fell by about two-thirds while the number of orders more than doubled, and the payroll rate barely moved, held in place by the recurring test.

From the matrix, a drill-through page lists the documents behind any test, so a reviewer can move from a dark cell to the exceptions in it, as Chapter 8 promised. What the reviewer then concludes about each exception, and how those conclusions are kept from month to month, is the subject of the section after the next tutorial.


{{< include _tutorial-02.qmd >}}


## Reviewing Exceptions

Each exception needs a disposition, Chapter 8's term for the auditor's conclusion about it: expected, with the evidence that explains it; follow up, with the question to ask; or a misstatement or control deficiency to report. Chapter 8 kept its dispositions on a worksheet of pasted values, because text typed beside a query's output can end up beside a different row when the query is refreshed. A monitoring report meets the same problem every month, since the register is rebuilt at each refresh. The answer is to keep the dispositions in a table of their own, keyed by the test and the document, and to merge them into the register. Each refresh then attaches every conclusion to the exception it concerns, and an exception that is new this month arrives with none. The exceptions without a disposition are the open exceptions, the reviewer's work for the month.

The dispositions are internal audit's record and need the same care as any audit workpaper. Only the reviewers change them, each conclusion should show who reached it and when, and the chief audit executive reviews them. A disposition recorded against the wrong document closes nothing while seeming to, so the register is tested to confirm that every disposition found its exception.

Even with dispositions, a monitoring system can raise more exceptions than its reviewers can examine. The volume of exceptions a continuous auditing system generates can overwhelm an internal audit department (Li et al., 2016), and Alles et al. (2006) found that preventing such alarm floods was one of the critical tasks in implementing continuous monitoring at Siemens. Li et al. (2016) proposed a framework that gives each exception a suspicion score from the rules it fails, has the auditors investigate the exceptions in the order of their scores, and updates the confidence placed in each rule as the investigations show which exceptions were errors or fraud. A simpler version of the same idea serves a small register: a document that fails several tests comes before one that fails a single test, the reasoning behind Chapter 8's risk score, and an exception that is new this month comes before one whose explanation is already on file.

Two kinds of exception should not be reviewed one document at a time. An exception expected every period, such as the year-end closing entries that exceed every approver's limit, needs its disposition and evidence once, and then only a check that it recurs as expected. An exception that recurs because of the design of a control, such as the registers approved by the employee they pay, is one finding, not dozens. The response is a change to the control, reported once, after which the exceptions should stop. Reviewing them one by one would only bury the new exceptions among the old.

Counting exceptions by approver shows who approved the documents that failed. It does not show how much of a process rests on one person, which needs the population: the share of each process's documents that each employee approved. At Charles River, one employee approved every payroll register and another nearly every purchase order, a concentration that no single exception reveals. Exercise 16.6 measures it.


## Auditing the Report Itself

Internal audit's monitoring report and the controller's package are both evidence that someone relies on, and neither is better than the data and the calculations behind it. Chapter 12 began every test with a reconciliation, because a query run against an incomplete table can report a clean result that means nothing, and a report is no different. Before relying on a report's numbers, an auditor asks of it the questions asked of any system that produces evidence, and @tbl-16-03 shows where a Power BI report keeps the answers. One more question, who can see the report, belongs with how it is published and shared, in [the appendix on publishing and security](#sec-appendix-publishing).

| Question | Evidence | In the reports of this Part |
|----------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Is every document in the model? | Each population reconciled to the ledger, and document numbers checked for gaps | Tests 1 and 4 of the monitoring file; the Validation pages |
| Do the measures compute what they claim? | Queries that reproduce totals known from other tools | The package's Tests 1 to 5; Test 2 of the monitoring file |
| How current are the data? | The last date of each population, and the refresh history | The Data Through card; the package's About page |
| Who changed the report, and was the change reviewed? | The version history of the report's files, and a record of approvals | A Power BI project under version control |

: The questions an auditor asks of a report {#tbl-16-03}

The first two questions already have answers. Test 1 of Tutorial 16.1 reconciled the journal entries to their postings, and the package's Tests tab, begun in Chapter 14, reproduces control totals of Chapters 6, 7, and 11, as the control totals of Chapter 4 checked a workbook. A population with nothing in the model to reconcile it to can still be tested for completeness. Charles River numbers its purchase orders in one series that runs across the years, as Exercise 8.5 found, so a count equal to the last number shows that none is missing, the gap test of Chapter 8. What any test shows depends on when it last ran: a test that passed in April says nothing about a measure changed in May. Rerunning the tests is part of every review, and their results, with the date they were run, belong in the audit workpaper.

The third question is easy to overlook. A report shows the data of its last refresh, and each population has its own last date. In Charles River's data, the journal entries and the purchase orders run to the last day of fiscal 2026, but the last payroll was paid on December 18, because the year's last pay periods are still open, as Chapter 12 found. A monitoring page for December that shows no payroll exceptions after the 18th has not tested those days at all. A measure that returns the earliest of the populations' last dates, shown on the page, states the date through which every test has run, as the package's About page states the period its data cover.

The fourth question concerns the report itself. A report that managers act on every month is a system, and changes to it deserve the change controls auditors expect of any system: each change to a query, a relationship, or a measure is requested, tested, approved, and recorded before readers see it, and the person who approves a change is not the one who made it. A .pbix file is a single binary file, so two copies can differ in one measure with nothing to show where. Saving the report as a Power BI project, a .pbip, stores the model and the report as folders of text files that version-control tools such as Git can keep and compare line by line (Microsoft, 2026b). A reviewer then sees each change as the lines it altered, and the Tests tab, rerun before the change is published, becomes the report's regression test, the check that a change has not broken what worked before.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A copy of a .pbix file holds a full copy of the model's data, every row of every table, whatever its pages show. A copy sent to a colleague or saved to a shared drive escapes every control in this chapter: its data stop at the date of the copy, its measures can drift from the version readers use, and whoever opens it in Power BI Desktop sees everything. Treat the report under change control as the only version, and when you audit a report, ask who holds copies of it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Teams that keep reports as Power BI projects often manage them as programmers manage code. Each change is made on a branch of a Git repository and reviewed by a colleague as a list of changed lines before it is merged and published, and the repository's history shows who changed what, when, and with whose approval. An auditor testing change control asks for that history and compares it with the published report, much as Chapter 12's saved scripts let a reviewer rerun and compare the audit queries. Sensitivity labels, which classify a report, are not supported in projects (Microsoft, 2026b), a tradeoff the appendix on publishing and security describes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
Every Part of this book has ended its tool's work with a way to make results checkable: the Documentation worksheet and control totals of Chapter 4, the saved scripts and audit query library of Part III, and the About page and Tests tab of Chapters 14 and 15. This chapter turns the auditor's eye on that discipline. Control totals are evidence only if they are rerun, tests only if the report they test is the one readers use, and documentation only if it states how current the data are. Auditing a report means checking that each of these still holds.
:::

## Looking Ahead

This chapter has turned the tests of Chapters 8 and 12 into monitoring. You built an exception register that runs the rule tests of three processes with every refresh, set each count beside its population, and found two patterns that call for different responses: exceptions that cluster in the first month of every year, and one that recurs every month because a control has no one to perform it. You recorded dispositions that survive every refresh, so that each month's review starts from the exceptions still open, and put first the documents that fail several tests. And you audited the reports themselves. Their populations are complete, their tests reproduce the results of earlier Parts, their data are current only to a date that differs by process, and their changes need controls that a single file cannot provide. Most of this work was descriptive and diagnostic analytics, in the terms of @tbl-01-01, and its recommendations, on the controls and on the reports, are prescriptive.

This chapter completes Part IV. Across its four chapters you have built a model from the Charles River workbook, measured it with DAX, turned it into a reporting package for its managers, and monitored and audited it for internal audit. How the package and the monitoring report reach their readers, and how each reader sees only what they should, is the subject of [the appendix on publishing and security](#sec-appendix-publishing), which you can work through in Power BI Desktop and, with a license, in the Power BI service. Part IV closes with a comprehensive case, and Part V then turns to integrated and applied topics that draw on every tool of the book.
